quick.summary: Stop asking users what they want, and start looking for what hurts.
quick.takeaway: Find real problems by watching users work and reading their complaints.

parts.title: Customer discovery

beats.line: I asked users what they wanted. Why is the new tool completely empty?
Because a doctor does not ask what pills you want.
They told me they wanted a shiny new dashboard.
You have to find their pain. Ask about their worst tasks instead.
Then watch them try to do those tasks.
We call this process continuous customer discovery.
Can I just say finding real problems?
Absolutely. We are finding real problems.
Okay. But what if they will not talk to me?

parts.cliff: We will hunt them down next time.

beats.line: Our sales team will not let me talk directly to the buyers.
That is very common. You have to start smaller.
Like asking the support team what people complain about?
Yes. Support tickets are a gold mine of pain.
You can also watch a sales call on mute.
So I do not need a giant formal interview every time.
A five minute chat with a user is better than guessing.
I will ask support for the ten worst complaints this week.
Now you are thinking like a true investigator.

quiz.question: How do you uncover a customer's real problem?
options: Watch them try to complete their hardest tasks.
Ask them what new features they want built.
Send them a survey with a list of our ideas.
Copy what a competitor is doing.
quiz.explanation: Customers often ask for solutions that do not fix their core issue. You have to find the pain by watching them struggle.

quiz.question: If you cannot speak to customers directly, it is impossible to learn about their problems.
quiz.explanation: You can always start small. Read support tickets or listen to sales calls to discover where users are frustrated.
